title: Why we forget the things we learn
reason: 昨天的课程聚焦网络技术与社会影响，今天轮换到学习方法和主动输出。本集解释为什么一次接触或考前突击很难留下长期记忆，以及重复、专注、建立联系和深度理解如何帮助记忆，直接对应“能够听懂或看懂，却难以及时调用”的瓶颈。练习会让六个高频表达先在客观题中重复出现，再逐步迁移到技术学习和日常表达。

targetExpressions.meaning: repeating something is essential for remembering or improving it
targetExpressions.usage: Use it to stress the importance of repeated practice: Repetition is key when you want a new phrase to become automatic.

targetExpressions.meaning: the probability or chance that something will happen
targetExpressions.usage: Use it before a noun or -ing form: The odds of remembering every detail after one reading are low.

targetExpressions.meaning: something that happens only once and is not repeated
targetExpressions.usage: Use it for a single event rather than a regular activity: The workshop was useful, but it was only a one-off.

targetExpressions.meaning: remain in someone's memory instead of being forgotten
targetExpressions.usage: Use it for information or experiences that stay memorable: A practical example is more likely to stick with me.

targetExpressions.meaning: connect new information with something already known
targetExpressions.usage: Use it to describe an association: I linked the new API concept to a system I had already built.

targetExpressions.expression: come up with new ways of looking at something
targetExpressions.meaning: develop different ideas or perspectives for understanding something
targetExpressions.usage: Use it when deeper understanding creates fresh perspectives: The team came up with new ways of looking at the recurring incident.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Complete the opening contrast: People may forget things they have read, while other information ______ them.
objectiveQuestions.explanation: The transcript says some information is easily forgotten while other, sometimes useless, information sticks with people.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Complete Dr Horvath's first rule for memory: ______.
objectiveQuestions.explanation: Dr Horvath states that repetition is the first key rule because a single exposure is rarely enough for long-term memory.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: What does “a one-off” mean in the discussion of memory?

options.text: A fact that everyone already understands
A memory recorded in a photograph

objectiveQuestions.explanation: The programme defines a one-off as something that happens only once.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Complete the idea: ______ remembering something after a one-off are incredibly slim.
objectiveQuestions.explanation: The odds of refers to probability; Dr Horvath says the probability of remembering a single exposure is very low.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Complete the memory strategy: Immediately ______ new information ______ something you already understand.
objectiveQuestions.explanation: Dr Horvath says an immediate connection to existing knowledge can make even a one-off memorable.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Why does the episode present exam cramming as a weak learning method?

options.text: It concentrates information into one short session instead of using repeated, focused learning.
It gives students too many opportunities to connect ideas.
It requires learners to explain ideas in several different ways.
It always produces a photographic memory.

objectiveQuestions.explanation: The transcript reports that students quickly forget most crammed material, supporting the rule that repetition and focus are important.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Which activity best represents deep learning as described in the episode?
objectiveQuestions.targetExpression: come up with new ways of looking at something

options.text: Explaining a smaller set of ideas deeply and finding new perspectives on them
Repeating a hundred facts without considering their meaning
Reading a list once immediately before an exam
Avoiding any connection with existing knowledge

objectiveQuestions.explanation: Dr Horvath contrasts memorising many facts with understanding fewer ideas deeply and coming up with new ways of looking at them.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Which sentence uses “a one-off” naturally in a workplace learning context?

options.text: The security briefing should not be a one-off; we need regular practice.
We one-off the security briefing every month.
The team was a one-off remembering the rule.
A one-off means the briefing happens continuously.

objectiveQuestions.explanation: A one-off is a single event, so contrasting it with regular practice is natural and accurate.

assessment.retellingPrompt: Without looking at the full transcript, retell the episode in 80–120 words using this structure: (1) problem—why a single exposure is easy to forget; (2) two memory rules—repetition, focus and links to existing knowledge; (3) contrast—cramming versus deep learning. Phrase bank: “repetition is key”, “link something to something”, “come up with new ways of looking at something”. Use at least two phrases naturally. Simple, accurate sentences are enough.
referencePoints: People often forget names or material they have read even though other information stays with them.
A one-off exposure is unlikely to be remembered unless it is connected immediately to something already understood.
Dr Horvath's two rules are that repetition is key and people remember what they focus on.
Students who cram for tests forget a large amount of what they studied soon afterwards.
Traditional memorisation can reproduce facts without showing real understanding.
Deep learning means understanding fewer ideas fully and being able to describe them or view them in new ways.
